projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Jack Stoner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: April 2nd, 1941.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: April 2nd, 1941. And I don't have it in my notes anywhere: You enlisted in what branch of the service?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: United States Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. So what can you tell me about your training?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Training, well, the training, of course it was still peacetime, but our commanding officer instructed us, or told us, whichever way you want to say it, that, "Fellas, you're in it for a haul, long haul. The country's going to go to war. Some of you are not going to come back," he says, "and I don't want to bull crap any of you guys. I want to tell you the honest truth." And we went through about, oh, I would say three months of hard training. Some of it was with live ammunition like they are doing today. This was at Fort Eustis, Virginia. We were the first troops to use that fort. It was nothing but a mud hole when we got there and we were knee-deep in mud. After three months, half of us went one place, I don't know where, and about half of us, the other 50 percent of us were sent to Angel Island, which is off the coast of California, across the bay from Alcatraz prison. Then we still didn't know where we were going, but we were shipped to Hawai'i. As we got off the ship in Hawai'i, we were separated. Some of us went to this post. Some went to the other posts. Everybody went to different posts. The ones who were six feet or taller were told they were going into the MPs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why would height matter?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, it certainly did. The big guys went to the MPs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And I happened to go to Camp Malakole, which was at Barbers Point in Hawai'i, which was right on the ocean. We were an anti-aircraft unit and we stayed there. It was nice there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About what time did you get to Hawai'i?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: That there, I think it was July of '41. Got there in '41. Normal duties, marching, rifle range, all typical soldier's duties.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was life like there in Hawai'i at that time?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: At peacetime it was nice. In fact, peacetime it was beautiful. We ate like kings. We were able to go swimming. We were right on the beach practically. We were able to go to town about once a week, if we were free of our duties.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that would be Honolulu, I assume.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah, well, in Honolulu.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What would you do when you went to town?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, what any soldiers; you went to the bars. Beers were 10 cents a piece. Shots I think were 15 cents. Of course I didn't drink that much, but I went along with the guys. Even then we didn't have much to spend because we were getting paid 21 dollars a month. Out of that 21 dollars, 6.50 went for our insurance, 4.50 went for our laundry, so we had 10 dollars to spend for the month. After we went to town one day, we were broke. And then December 7th came along. Before that -- I'm getting ahead of myself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, did you think when you were in Hawai'i -- you mentioned that they told you that the war was on the horizon there. Did you feel -- did you feel like war was imminent; that we were going to get into it?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Not until November 25th, 6th or 27th. When we were placed double alert, which meant instead of having 10 guards at our post, we -- it was doubled to 20. We couldn't leave the post. Nobody could go into town. Nobody could do anything but stay on the post. Then after a few days everybody forgot about it, it was over with, until the morning of the 7th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, did you have any idea, was there any tension that Pearl Harbor, Hawai'i was a potential target?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: None, but if you read that book that I have you'll know that everybody knew about it but us. The Germans knew. The British knew. Franklin D. Roosevelt knew we were going to --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Honolulu was a target?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: We were going to hit -- he knew it. You read this book. You see the Pearl Harbor, they had messages that they decoded. They all knew, but they let it happen. They blamed Short and Kimmel for something. They were the fall guys.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So they were claiming that the messages actually named Pearl Harbor as the target?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yes, they did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And they decided not to do anything about it?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: They wanted the country to go to war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Is that -- do you believe that?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yes. It's fact taken from records which were secretly hidden which they couldn't -- secrecy act, until they repealed it or enacted it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: They could not open the records until they did, and this book tells you all about it. And this book was written by two people that were there at the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and name those people so we have it on the tape.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Lieutenant Commander Kenneth Landis, U.S. Navy, retired, and Staff Sergeant Rex Gunn, U.S. Army, retired.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And the name of that book?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Deceit At Pearl Harbor. And those are the two people that wrote that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what were you doing on December 6th, the day before the attack?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: That I don't remember, but I know December 7th we were going -- I was walking to the mess hall for breakfast when we started being strafed. When we looked up, see the rising sun on the planes, we knew it wasn't our planes strafing us. So we got the hell out of the way as fast as we could and got where we -- I don't know where we were running, but we were running, and our colonel came out. At that time all ammunition was under lock and key. Nobody had live ammunition. As soon as it started, as soon as they started strafing, our colonel came out, our colonel, John Long, who is a wonderful guy, he unlocked the ammunition, doled out ammunition to everybody. We had our 155 anti-aircraft guns, which we hooked up and got down into the harbor, which was we were -- our station was west, Westloch Naval Ammunition Dump, where the torpedos were stored and where the Navy ammunition ships were docked for loading. We got down there as fast as we could, set up, set up our 50 caliber machine guns. One of our fellas got credit for shooting down one of the Jap planes. They dropped one bomb, a couple bombs trying to hit the ammo ship, NITRO, which was docked where we were, but they proved to be duds. Hadn't they been duds, I wouldn't be here telling you, talking to you. And they kept strafing us, and they left for about an hour, but an hour went by and a second wave came over. And we were fortunate; we didn't suffer any casualties. And that was the end of that day, but all night long the people, they were saying, "They are landing over here. They are landing over there. The Japs are landing here," which was all rumors. And then after we were there, I don't remember how long we were there, we were shipped to Guadalcanal. And first we did a little fighting on Guadalcanal. After Guadalcanal we wound up in Bougainville. Bougainville I think was tougher fight than Guadalcanal. The Japs were making -- trying to make some last stands, last ditch stands there. In fact, one of their generals was shot down over Bougainville, General Yamamoto, who was their head man, admiral or general.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Admiral, right.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Admiral Yamamoto.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And that was it, just about it. I got home in January of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Can you give me a little more detail about Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, Guadalcanal we tried to dig in as soon as you landed, but you couldn't dig in because as soon as you dug six inches, you ran into water because we were on the beach, but we did the best we could. We were getting shot at, we were shooting at them, and that was about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still with an anti-aircraft unit at that point?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah. They changed us to -- instead of anti-air -- yeah, we were still anti-aircraft.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: At first we were coast artillery in Hawai'i.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, okay.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Then we became anti-aircraft. See, we were stationed right on the coast, right on the coast in Hawai'i, at Barbers Point.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. What was your particular job?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I had two jobs. I was a mess sergeant, and I also was a gunnery sergeant. When we weren't coursing Guadalcanal or Bougainville, when we weren't able to do anything in the mess tent, we were out on the firing line with the rest of the troops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How often did that happen?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Quite often. Happened -- one of the places it happened more than anyplace else was Hill 700. I don't know if you ever read about Hill 700 in Bougainville, but they outnumbered us, but at the end we outnumbered them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of actual combat on the line? Was that at Guadalcanal?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: But "remember," not really. I don't think I remember any of that. All I remember is being glad the shooting stopped.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As a mess sergeant were the guys happy with the food that you fed them?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, we got what we were able to. We had no -- you know, we had no refrigeration, so when we first hit Guadalcanal we ate sea rations, which were left over from World War I. We couldn't light a fire, so in the morning we had little packets with a hard cracker, which you needed a sledgehammer to break, a can of beef stew -- see, I never told my sons any of this -- a little wafer that you had to dissolve for coffee, which you had no hot water because you couldn't light a fire, so you had to try to dissolve it in cold water, and that's what you drank. It's laughable now that it's all over, but at that time it wasn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you didn't have a lot of complaints; they were just glad to get something?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, they had no choice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you on Guadalcanal then?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, we were on Guadalcanal probably, I'm -- these are guesses, guessing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's fine, that's fine.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Probably eight months, maybe a year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And then we were on Bougainville, which was another one of the Sol -- larger Solomon Islands. We were there for about eight months, maybe a year, about another year. All together I was overseas for 39 months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other details that you can tell me about Bougainville?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, except at one time -- this is what we were told, we don't know for sure -- that those people were cannibals over there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No -- any evidence of that?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, no, not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And these would be the natives on Bougainville?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: These were the natives on Bougainville.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Of course you didn't see too much of the natives on Bougainville because they always hid. They were in the hills, in the mountains. There were mountains on Bougainville and they were up in the mountains hiding. They were hiding from the Japs more than they were hiding from us. They weren't scared of us, because we did not harm 'em, but the Japanese did -- would harm them if they seen them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else you can tell me about Bougainville?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. In fact, I see one of my close buddies -- he lives in Pittsburgh, I see him. We have a reunion every year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And if it's close by I try to make it. I've made it for the past 15 years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And there's about -- most of 'em that I see there now were replacements that I didn't even know, but now I see there's one -- let's see, there's six _____. There's about five of us that are -- were together at Pearl Harbor, and we're usually at our reunion, and we are together all the time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So do you remember anything that you and your buddies might have done to pass the time or for entertainment?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah. We gambled what we had, played cards if we had a chance, and there wasn't much else to do really. There wasn't much free time. Every night at Bougainville, I do remember this, Washing Machine Charlie would come over. We could hear him, but we couldn't see him, and every once in a while he'd drop a bomb or two.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So his mission was just harassment?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: That's all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Try to keep you from sleeping?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, it would at times.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Did you get any kind of shows or anything, any U.S.O. tours come through?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, we heard about 'em, but we didn't have any. In fact, I didn't see a WAC or a WAF until I got back to the states. We had the Red Cross over there once in a while, but I'd rather not talk about them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Problem with the Red Cross?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I'll talk about 'em if we weren't on --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: -- this, but I will not say anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. I've talked to some other guys that had difficulties with the Red Cross, so you're welcome to share that, but if you don't want to, that's fine.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, not on this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I would. I'll tell you about 'em --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: -- after.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Mail call, oh, that's what we waited for every day is mail call. I used to get the newspaper. My brother used to send me at -- one of the newspapers, I don't know if it was The News or The Press. Where did Frank work for first, News, Chris?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's here in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Um-hum. He used to send me The News, but by the time I got it, it was four to six weeks after the date, but it was still nice to get it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Did you get packages or anything?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, yeah. My sisters always sent me care packages. Sometimes I'd get 'em, sometimes I wouldn't get 'em.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any explanation of what happened to them when you didn't get them?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, nobody knew. Who knew what happened to them? Ship might have gone down with 'em, or maybe somebody stole 'em. We never knew that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's not like you found out you were missing good food packages?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, we were, and my buddy, Johnny Salamon, (ph) used to get food packages from his parents in New York. We were -- we got -- well, we all split. We divvied up whatever we got. We always split. None of us were hogs about it. One guy got something, whoever was around got part of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have a girlfriend at that time?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Um-hum, right there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did she write a lot?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: (No audible response.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did she write a lot to you?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: (Inaudible response.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kinds of things would she write?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Just normal things, what was happening. That was my wife until she passed away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Chris' mom.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to write much to her?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I used to try to write about -- I never was much for writing letters, but we had that, what they call V mail.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: And I'd write about once a week, maybe oftener, whenever you had time to sit down and write.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you couldn't really tell her where you were?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No. If you did, it was cut out. It was all censored. You couldn't tell anybody where you were, or all they knew was you were in the Pacific. That was as far as you could go. Well, they knew that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't think we mentioned your outfit. What outfit was it?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: It was originally the 251 Coast Artillery. Then later on we were merged into the 746th Coast Artillery, anti-aircraft. That's when we became anti-aircraft when we start getting replacements in, and there was two of us outfits were merged and made into one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's go back to Pearl Harbor. How close to the harbor were you set up on that day, on December 7th?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: When we set up, we were in the harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So you could see the ships in the harbor, the whole thing?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Pardon? We were right there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: We were at the ammunition dump, which was called Westloch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: W-E-S-T-L-O-C-H.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. I've been to Pearl Harbor. I'm trying to figure out where that would be, probably on the opposite side away from the Arizona.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Did you see the Arizona take the big hit?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I seen it all. Well, we didn't see 'em take the hits, but we could see all the smoke coming. We seen some of 'em get hit, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you think, I mean, you probably were doing your job, but when you saw what was happening?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: You didn't know what to think. You were in shock. You were in shock. You were scared. Anybody tells you they weren't scared is full of shit, full of hot air.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: We were kids, you know, all of us were. We were kids at the time. We didn't -- we didn't know if we were ever going to come back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you said you mentioned about being strafed. What was going through your mind the first time when that happened, when you were strafed?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I don't think you had time to think. You just went about and tried to do what you had to do. If you start thinking, you wouldn't know what to do, but you didn't have time to think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about after the attack, when you saw what had happened?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah, you were in shock. You couldn't -- it was unbelievable.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there any kind of feeling in your mind like, "How can we ever recover from this?"

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Well, you all -- so many things go through your mind. You don't remember what went through your mind. Everything goes through your mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, did you get along -- before the attack did you get along okay with the Japanese Americans on the island?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah, oh, yeah. We had no trouble with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about after?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Even after, huh-uh. Most of 'em, in fact I would say 99 percent of them were -- wound up being U.S. citizens anyway. They were loyal to America, at least I thought they were.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So there wasn't -- well, did you see that in your outfit, though? Was there much resentment or paranoia about --

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, no, we had none whatsoever that I ever seen, huh-uh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever hear about any incidents of espionage or sabotage?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, you heard about espionage, but you don't -- you try to separate fact from fiction, and most of it was fiction. You heard that there was somebody in this building that was way up that was spying, and you heard this and that, but it got so you didn't, you didn't believe it because it wasn't true. Like I say, it was rumors.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you lose any buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything you want to tell me about that?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. So when did you come home?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I got home in January of '45 from overseas. I was shipped down to Miami Beach for R and R. I was shipped there for two weeks, supposed to be two weeks for R and R, and I was assigned permanent party there until July of '45. July of '45 I was discharged, July 30th to be exact.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You remember the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Yeah, because my wife was -- wasn't my wife at the time yet -- was coming down for to us get married down in Florida. She was on the train coming down to Florida when he passed away, so I remember that very distinctly.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction that you saw around you?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: One of sorrow.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where would you have been on VE Day? That would be in May.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: May, well, I was in Florida.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I was stationed in Florida then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything, any wild celebrations or anything happen that night?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, because we kind of figured it was coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Because they were starting to send more and more troops back from overseas, so we knew. We kind of -- we kind of figured, you know, something was coming.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And let's see, VJD, you were out of the --

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: VJ Day I was out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were back in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I was home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What can you -- can you tell me about VJ Day in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: VJ Day in Cleveland, yeah. We were -- I was with my wife. We were in one of the department stores looking for something, I forget what it was, and I was sitting there waiting on -- of course my wife shopped, you know. I was sitting there close to where she was shopping, and two, two old ladies -- well, to me they were old at the time. My wife heard them mention, "Why isn't he in the service? Look at that young guy. He's setting there." My wife went up to 'em. She -- oh, did she tell them off.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: I says, "What did you do that for?" She said, "Them son of a B's, they wanted to know why you weren't in the service." I says, "You should have told them I was 4-F."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't matter to you, huh?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, I didn't care what any -- what they thought. I knew what I was did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So that actually happened on VJ Day or --

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Um-hum, on VJ Day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do to celebrate the final end of the war?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: We didn't. I didn't do anything. We didn't do -- we were just happy it was over with.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: We went home and we were happy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there ever a point during the war that you thought maybe America would loose?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, never, never, especially after the Battle of Midway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you then, do you --

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: In Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So it looked like we had it all along. The question just drifted out of my mind. Oh, did you have any trouble adjusting to civilian life after the war?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't have any problem with --

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Hum-um.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- bad dreams or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Once in a while you dream, you know, but not continually. Once in a while you still dream about your friends or things that happened, you know, but that's -- I think that's normal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: No, nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That jumps out.

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Just that I was wished I was back home, which I think we all wished.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay. This isn't one of my questions, but I saw this on a different question list somewhere. What did you think you were fighting for during World War II?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: You know, to be honest, we didn't know. We didn't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know when the war was over what you had been fighting for?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Hell, no. We fought to rebuild Japan, make them a world power.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're not sure what you accomplished?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Not really, huh-uh, especially when they talk about war today, which I'm dead set against.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything else?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: Nope that's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That covers it?

sp.speaker: Jack Stoner
sp.p: That covers it. SWOPE: Very good. You seem like you've done this before. You've been interviewed before, haven't you? STONER: Oh, by what's her name, yeah, a few times. END OF CD. TRANSCRIBER'S NOTE: Chris {Stoner} also present.
